case_info.scenario: A 71-year-old man presented to the dermatologist with a 6-week history of a rapidly progressing rash and swelling of the left side of the chest wall. He had noticed the rash a few days after receiving the second dose of an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine (Moderna). He denied itching, weeping, bleeding, or discharge from the rash or the nipple. He had a history of metabolic syndrome treated with antihypertensives and oral hypoglycemics. The physical examination showed a morbidly obese White man. The skin examination showed a 19 × 10-cm pink, fallacious purple color deep-infiltrated papule in the left breast and a similar 15 × 7-cm papule under the left clavicle (Figure, A). The breast examination was notable for bilateral gynecomastia and inverted left nipple without any palpable lumps. No lymphadenopathy was noted either. His laboratory results showed stage 2 chronic kidney disease. Results of a viral panel including hepatitis A, B, and C and HIV were negative. The punch biopsy of the skin showed a diffuse island of atypical cells in the dermis (Figure, B). On immunohistochemical staining, the atypical cells stained positive for CK-7, GATA-3, and PAX-8 (weak focal staining) and negative for estrogen receptor (ER)/progesterone receptor (<1%), TTF-1, SATB-2, CDX-2, and NKX-3.1. The positron emission tomography–computed tomography scan showed a diffuse, infiltrating fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-avid cutaneous lesion on the left chest wall (standardized uptake value, 6.5) and multiple FDG-avid nodes in the axilla (bilaterally), left internal mammary, and left cervical chain. The core biopsy from the lymph node is shown in theFigure, C.
case_info.caption: A, Rash on the left chest wall. B and C, Hematoxylin-eosin stains of the punch biopsy of the skin and core biopsy of the lymph node, respectively (both original magnification ×10).
case_info.explanation: The histopathological findings of the lymph node biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma with micropapillary features. The immunohistochemical staining was positive for GATA-3 and CK-7, along with 40% ER expression. Next-generation sequencing showed a microsatellite stable status and variations in theCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CAgenes. Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) with invasive ductal carcinoma and treated with systemic chemotherapy. It is important to note that the history of receiving the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine is a red herring in this case. It is challenging to differentiate between adnexal tumors and breast cancer when the patient presents with a cutaneous lesion of the breast. The current patient presented with a widespread rash, retracted nipple, and a peau d’orange appearance of the skin commonly seen in patients with IBC.1However, peau d’orange skin can also be seen in patients with cellulitis and radiation-induced lymphatic blockage.2The atypical cells obtained from a skin punch biopsy stained positive for GATA-3 and CK-7. GATA-3 belongs to the GATA family of zinc-finger transcription and is involved in the development and morphogenesis of breast tissue.3It is commonly expressed in ER-positive breast cancers. However, the expression of GATA-3 is not exclusive to breast cancer and has been reported in tumors of the salivary gland, urothelial system, skin and adnexa, mesothelioma, and pancreas.4Breast glands are considered to be modified and highly specialized apocrine glands. Hence, they share structural and functional homology with sweat glands.5 In addition to staining positive for GATA-3, adnexal tumors stain positive for P63, CK5/6, and CK-7. The clinical picture of the current patient was challenging due to the lack of a discrete breast mass and a positron emission tomography scan demonstrating an FDG-avid infiltrating mass in the chest wall and several lymph nodes in the axillary and internal mammary chain. A core-needle biopsy of the chest wall mass showed a similar staining pattern but stained positive for ER, unlike the punch biopsy of the skin, which was negative for both ER and progesterone receptor. However, a positive ER status alone is not sufficient to differentiate between an adnexal gland tumor and breast cancer.6The diagnosis was finally established with the results of the positive molecular testing forCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CA. The phosphatidylinositol-3-kinases-CA (PIK3CA) variation is highly associated with ER-positive/ERBB2-negative breast cancer.7Likewise, ERBB2 (also known as HER2 or neu) is expressed in 30% of breast cancers.8Limited studies in patients with adnexal gland tumors reported no expression ofPIK3CAorERBB2in such patients.9Hence, the current patient’s pattern of the molecular profile of tumor tissue was most consistent with carcinoma of breast origin. Breast cancer in men accounts for 1% of all breast cancers.10Inflammatory breast cancer is an aggressive form of breast cancer that accounts for 2% to 4% of all breast cancers and 7% to 10% of breast cancer mortality in the US. The majority of men with breast cancer present with retroareolar mass. The usual presenting features are skin ulceration, retraction, bleeding from the nipple, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Inflammatory breast cancer in men is extremely rare, and the diagnosis is often made at an advanced stage due to lack of screening guidelines and confusion with gynecomastia (common in obese men). Although signs of inflammation (erythema, warmth, tenderness) are noted in the majority of patients, a few patients may present with painless skin induration due to lymphatic invasion of the dermis. The involvement of dermal lymphatics is associated with poor prognosis and is a contraindication to surgery as an initial management, regardless of the extent.10This report highlights the importance of using the complete clinicopathologic features, including tumor morphologic characteristics, immunohistochemical staining, and molecular profiling, to arrive at the correct diagnosis.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: The histopathological findings of the lymph node biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma with micropapillary features. The immunohistochemical staining was positive for GATA-3 and CK-7, along with 40% ER expression. Next-generation sequencing showed a microsatellite stable status and variations in theCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CAgenes. Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) with invasive ductal carcinoma and treated with systemic chemotherapy. It is important to note that the history of receiving the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine is a red herring in this case. It is challenging to differentiate between adnexal tumors and breast cancer when the patient presents with a cutaneous lesion of the breast. The current patient presented with a widespread rash, retracted nipple, and a peau d’orange appearance of the skin commonly seen in patients with IBC.1However, peau d’orange skin can also be seen in patients with cellulitis and radiation-induced lymphatic blockage.2The atypical cells obtained from a skin punch biopsy stained positive for GATA-3 and CK-7. GATA-3 belongs to the GATA family of zinc-finger transcription and is involved in the development and morphogenesis of breast tissue.3It is commonly expressed in ER-positive breast cancers. However, the expression of GATA-3 is not exclusive to breast cancer and has been reported in tumors of the salivary gland, urothelial system, skin and adnexa, mesothelioma, and pancreas.4Breast glands are considered to be modified and highly specialized apocrine glands. Hence, they share structural and functional homology with sweat glands.5 In addition to staining positive for GATA-3, adnexal tumors stain positive for P63, CK5/6, and CK-7. The clinical picture of the current patient was challenging due to the lack of a discrete breast mass and a positron emission tomography scan demonstrating an FDG-avid infiltrating mass in the chest wall and several lymph nodes in the axillary and internal mammary chain. The phosphatidylinositol-3-kinases-CA (PIK3CA) variation is highly associated with ER-positive/ERBB2-negative breast cancer.7Likewise, ERBB2 (also known as HER2 or neu) is expressed in 30% of breast cancers.8Limited studies in patients with adnexal gland tumors reported no expression ofPIK3CAorERBB2in such patients.9Hence, the current patient’s pattern of the molecular profile of tumor tissue was most consistent with carcinoma of breast origin. Breast cancer in men accounts for 1% of all breast cancers.10Inflammatory breast cancer is an aggressive form of breast cancer that accounts for 2% to 4% of all breast cancers and 7% to 10% of breast cancer mortality in the US. The majority of men with breast cancer present with retroareolar mass. The usual presenting features are skin ulceration, retraction, bleeding from the nipple, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Inflammatory breast cancer in men is extremely rare, and the diagnosis is often made at an advanced stage due to lack of screening guidelines and confusion with gynecomastia (common in obese men). Although signs of inflammation (erythema, warmth, tenderness) are noted in the majority of patients, a few patients may present with painless skin induration due to lymphatic invasion of the dermis. The involvement of dermal lymphatics is associated with poor prognosis and is a contraindication to surgery as an initial management, regardless of the extent.10This report highlights the importance of using the complete clinicopathologic features, including tumor morphologic characteristics, immunohistochemical staining, and molecular profiling, to arrive at the correct diagnosis.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.caption: A, Rash on the left chest wall. B and C, Hematoxylin-eosin stains of the punch biopsy of the skin and core biopsy of the lymph node, respectively (both original magnification ×10).
case_info.explanation: The histopathological findings of the lymph node biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma with micropapillary features. The immunohistochemical staining was positive for GATA-3 and CK-7, along with 40% ER expression. Next-generation sequencing showed a microsatellite stable status and variations in theCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CAgenes. Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) with invasive ductal carcinoma and treated with systemic chemotherapy. It is important to note that the history of receiving the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine is a red herring in this case. It is challenging to differentiate between adnexal tumors and breast cancer when the patient presents with a cutaneous lesion of the breast. The current patient presented with a widespread rash, retracted nipple, and a peau d’orange appearance of the skin commonly seen in patients with IBC.1However, peau d’orange skin can also be seen in patients with cellulitis and radiation-induced lymphatic blockage.2The atypical cells obtained from a skin punch biopsy stained positive for GATA-3 and CK-7. GATA-3 belongs to the GATA family of zinc-finger transcription and is involved in the development and morphogenesis of breast tissue.3It is commonly expressed in ER-positive breast cancers. However, the expression of GATA-3 is not exclusive to breast cancer and has been reported in tumors of the salivary gland, urothelial system, skin and adnexa, mesothelioma, and pancreas.4Breast glands are considered to be modified and highly specialized apocrine glands. Hence, they share structural and functional homology with sweat glands.5 In addition to staining positive for GATA-3, adnexal tumors stain positive for P63, CK5/6, and CK-7. The clinical picture of the current patient was challenging due to the lack of a discrete breast mass and a positron emission tomography scan demonstrating an FDG-avid infiltrating mass in the chest wall and several lymph nodes in the axillary and internal mammary chain. A core-needle biopsy of the chest wall mass showed a similar staining pattern but stained positive for ER, unlike the punch biopsy of the skin, which was negative for both ER and progesterone receptor. However, a positive ER status alone is not sufficient to differentiate between an adnexal gland tumor and breast cancer.6The diagnosis was finally established with the results of the positive molecular testing forCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CA. The phosphatidylinositol-3-kinases-CA (PIK3CA) variation is highly associated with ER-positive/ERBB2-negative breast cancer.7Likewise, ERBB2 (also known as HER2 or neu) is expressed in 30% of breast cancers.8Limited studies in patients with adnexal gland tumors reported no expression ofPIK3CAorERBB2in such patients.9Hence, the current patient’s pattern of the molecular profile of tumor tissue was most consistent with carcinoma of breast origin. Breast cancer in men accounts for 1% of all breast cancers.10Inflammatory breast cancer is an aggressive form of breast cancer that accounts for 2% to 4% of all breast cancers and 7% to 10% of breast cancer mortality in the US. The majority of men with breast cancer present with retroareolar mass. The usual presenting features are skin ulceration, retraction, bleeding from the nipple, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Inflammatory breast cancer in men is extremely rare, and the diagnosis is often made at an advanced stage due to lack of screening guidelines and confusion with gynecomastia (common in obese men). Although signs of inflammation (erythema, warmth, tenderness) are noted in the majority of patients, a few patients may present with painless skin induration due to lymphatic invasion of the dermis. The involvement of dermal lymphatics is associated with poor prognosis and is a contraindication to surgery as an initial management, regardless of the extent.10This report highlights the importance of using the complete clinicopathologic features, including tumor morphologic characteristics, immunohistochemical staining, and molecular profiling, to arrive at the correct diagnosis.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",

    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },

  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule

       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or

case_info.explanation: The histopathological findings of the lymph node biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma with micropapillary features. The immunohistochemical staining was positive for GATA-3 and CK-7, along with 40% ER expression. Next-generation sequencing showed a microsatellite stable status and variations in theCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CAgenes. Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) with invasive ductal carcinoma and treated with systemic chemotherapy. It is important to note that the history of receiving the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine is a red herring in this case. It is challenging to differentiate between adnexal tumors and breast cancer when the patient presents with a cutaneous lesion of the breast. The current patient presented with a widespread rash, retracted nipple, and a peau d’orange appearance of the skin commonly seen in patients with IBC.1However, peau d’orange skin can also be seen in patients with cellulitis and radiation-induced lymphatic blockage.2The atypical cells obtained from a skin punch biopsy stained positive for GATA-3 and CK-7. GATA-3 belongs to the GATA family of zinc-finger transcription and is involved in the development and morphogenesis of breast tissue.3It is commonly expressed in ER-positive breast cancers. However, the expression of GATA-3 is not exclusive to breast cancer and has been reported in tumors of the salivary gland, urothelial system, skin and adnexa, mesothelioma, and pancreas.4Breast glands are considered to be modified and highly specialized apocrine glands. Hence, they share structural and functional homology with sweat glands.5 In addition to staining positive for GATA-3, adnexal tumors stain positive for P63, CK5/6, and CK-7. The clinical picture of the current patient was challenging due to the lack of a discrete breast mass and a positron emission tomography scan demonstrating an FDG-avid infiltrating mass in the chest wall and several lymph nodes in the axillary and internal mammary chain. A core-needle biopsy of the chest wall mass showed a similar staining pattern but stained positive for ER, unlike the punch biopsy of the skin, which was negative for both ER and progesterone receptor. However, a positive ER status alone is not sufficient to differentiate between an adnexal gland tumor and breast cancer.6The diagnosis was finally established with the results of the positive molecular testing forCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CA. The phosphatidylinositol-3-kinases-CA (PIK3CA) variation is highly associated with ER-positive/ERBB2-negative breast cancer.7Likewise, ERBB2 (also known as HER2 or neu) is expressed in 30% of breast cancers.8Limited studies in patients with adnexal gland tumors reported no expression ofPIK3CAorERBB2in such patients.9Hence, the current patient’s pattern of the molecular profile of tumor tissue was most consistent with carcinoma of breast origin. Breast cancer in men accounts for 1% of all breast cancers.10Inflammatory breast cancer is an aggressive form of breast cancer that accounts for 2% to 4% of all breast cancers and 7% to 10% of breast cancer mortality in the US. The majority of men with breast cancer present with retroareolar mass. The usual presenting features are skin ulceration, retraction, bleeding from the nipple, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Inflammatory breast cancer in men is extremely rare, and the diagnosis is often made at an advanced stage due to lack of screening guidelines and confusion with gynecomastia (common in obese men). You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

case_info.scenario: A 71-year-old man presented to the dermatologist with a 6-week history of a rapidly progressing rash and swelling of the left side of the chest wall. He had noticed the rash a few days after receiving the second dose of an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine (Moderna). He denied itching, weeping, bleeding, or discharge from the rash or the nipple. He had a history of metabolic syndrome treated with antihypertensives and oral hypoglycemics. The physical examination showed a morbidly obese White man. The skin examination showed a 19 × 10-cm pink, fallacious purple color deep-infiltrated papule in the left breast and a similar 15 × 7-cm papule under the left clavicle (Figure, A). The breast examination was notable for bilateral gynecomastia and inverted left nipple without any palpable lumps. No lymphadenopathy was noted either. His laboratory results showed stage 2 chronic kidney disease. Results of a viral panel including hepatitis A, B, and C and HIV were negative. The punch biopsy of the skin showed a diffuse island of atypical cells in the dermis (Figure, B). On immunohistochemical staining, the atypical cells stained positive for CK-7, GATA-3, and PAX-8 (weak focal staining) and negative for estrogen receptor (ER)/progesterone receptor (<1%), TTF-1, SATB-2, CDX-2, and NKX-3.1. The positron emission tomography–computed tomography scan showed a diffuse, infiltrating fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-avid cutaneous lesion on the left chest wall (standardized uptake value, 6.5) and multiple FDG-avid nodes in the axilla (bilaterally), left internal mammary, and left cervical chain. The core biopsy from the lymph node is shown in theFigure, C.

case_info.explanation: The histopathological findings of the lymph node biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma with micropapillary features. The immunohistochemical staining was positive for GATA-3 and CK-7, along with 40% ER expression. Next-generation sequencing showed a microsatellite stable status and variations in theCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CAgenes. Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) with invasive ductal carcinoma and treated with systemic chemotherapy. It is important to note that the history of receiving the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine is a red herring in this case. It is challenging to differentiate between adnexal tumors and breast cancer when the patient presents with a cutaneous lesion of the breast. The current patient presented with a widespread rash, retracted nipple, and a peau d’orange appearance of the skin commonly seen in patients with IBC.1However, peau d’orange skin can also be seen in patients with cellulitis and radiation-induced lymphatic blockage.2The atypical cells obtained from a skin punch biopsy stained positive for GATA-3 and CK-7. GATA-3 belongs to the GATA family of zinc-finger transcription and is involved in the development and morphogenesis of breast tissue.3It is commonly expressed in ER-positive breast cancers. However, the expression of GATA-3 is not exclusive to breast cancer and has been reported in tumors of the salivary gland, urothelial system, skin and adnexa, mesothelioma, and pancreas.4Breast glands are considered to be modified and highly specialized apocrine glands. Hence, they share structural and functional homology with sweat glands.5 In addition to staining positive for GATA-3, adnexal tumors stain positive for P63, CK5/6, and CK-7. The clinical picture of the current patient was challenging due to the lack of a discrete breast mass and a positron emission tomography scan demonstrating an FDG-avid infiltrating mass in the chest wall and several lymph nodes in the axillary and internal mammary chain. A core-needle biopsy of the chest wall mass showed a similar staining pattern but stained positive for ER, unlike the punch biopsy of the skin, which was negative for both ER and progesterone receptor. However, a positive ER status alone is not sufficient to differentiate between an adnexal gland tumor and breast cancer.6The diagnosis was finally established with the results of the positive molecular testing forCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CA. The phosphatidylinositol-3-kinases-CA (PIK3CA) variation is highly associated with ER-positive/ERBB2-negative breast cancer.7Likewise, ERBB2 (also known as HER2 or neu) is expressed in 30% of breast cancers.8Limited studies in patients with adnexal gland tumors reported no expression ofPIK3CAorERBB2in such patients.9Hence, the current patient’s pattern of the molecular profile of tumor tissue was most consistent with carcinoma of breast origin. Breast cancer in men accounts for 1% of all breast cancers.10Inflammatory breast cancer is an aggressive form of breast cancer that accounts for 2% to 4% of all breast cancers and 7% to 10% of breast cancer mortality in the US. The majority of men with breast cancer present with retroareolar mass. The usual presenting features are skin ulceration, retraction, bleeding from the nipple, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Inflammatory breast cancer in men is extremely rare, and the diagnosis is often made at an advanced stage due to lack of screening guidelines and confusion with gynecomastia (common in obese men). Although signs of inflammation (erythema, warmth, tenderness) are noted in the majority of patients, a few patients may present with painless skin induration due to lymphatic invasion of the dermis. The involvement of dermal lymphatics is associated with poor prognosis and is a contraindication to surgery as an initial management, regardless of the extent.10This report highlights the importance of using the complete clinicopathologic features, including tumor morphologic characteristics, immunohistochemical staining, and molecular profiling, to arrive at the correct diagnosis.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: The histopathological findings of the lymph node biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma with micropapillary features. The immunohistochemical staining was positive for GATA-3 and CK-7, along with 40% ER expression. Next-generation sequencing showed a microsatellite stable status and variations in theCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CAgenes. Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) with invasive ductal carcinoma and treated with systemic chemotherapy. It is important to note that the history of receiving the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine is a red herring in this case. It is challenging to differentiate between adnexal tumors and breast cancer when the patient presents with a cutaneous lesion of the breast. The current patient presented with a widespread rash, retracted nipple, and a peau d’orange appearance of the skin commonly seen in patients with IBC.1However, peau d’orange skin can also be seen in patients with cellulitis and radiation-induced lymphatic blockage.2The atypical cells obtained from a skin punch biopsy stained positive for GATA-3 and CK-7. GATA-3 belongs to the GATA family of zinc-finger transcription and is involved in the development and morphogenesis of breast tissue.3It is commonly expressed in ER-positive breast cancers. However, the expression of GATA-3 is not exclusive to breast cancer and has been reported in tumors of the salivary gland, urothelial system, skin and adnexa, mesothelioma, and pancreas.4Breast glands are considered to be modified and highly specialized apocrine glands. Hence, they share structural and functional homology with sweat glands.5 In addition to staining positive for GATA-3, adnexal tumors stain positive for P63, CK5/6, and CK-7. The clinical picture of the current patient was challenging due to the lack of a discrete breast mass and a positron emission tomography scan demonstrating an FDG-avid infiltrating mass in the chest wall and several lymph nodes in the axillary and internal mammary chain. A core-needle biopsy of the chest wall mass showed a similar staining pattern but stained positive for ER, unlike the punch biopsy of the skin, which was negative for both ER and progesterone receptor. However, a positive ER status alone is not sufficient to differentiate between an adnexal gland tumor and breast cancer.6The diagnosis was finally established with the results of the positive molecular testing forCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CA. The phosphatidylinositol-3-kinases-CA (PIK3CA) variation is highly associated with ER-positive/ERBB2-negative breast cancer.7Likewise, ERBB2 (also known as HER2 or neu) is expressed in 30% of breast cancers.8Limited studies in patients with adnexal gland tumors reported no expression ofPIK3CAorERBB2in such patients.9Hence, the current patient’s pattern of the molecular profile of tumor tissue was most consistent with carcinoma of breast origin. Breast cancer in men accounts for 1% of all breast cancers.10Inflammatory breast cancer is an aggressive form of breast cancer that accounts for 2% to 4% of all breast cancers and 7% to 10% of breast cancer mortality in the US. The majority of men with breast cancer present with retroareolar mass. The usual presenting features are skin ulceration, retraction, bleeding from the nipple, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Inflammatory breast cancer in men is extremely rare, and the diagnosis is often made at an advanced stage due to lack of screening guidelines and confusion with gynecomastia (common in obese men). Although signs of inflammation (erythema, warmth, tenderness) are noted in the majority of patients, a few patients may present with painless skin induration due to lymphatic invasion of the dermis. The involvement of dermal lymphatics is associated with poor prognosis and is a contraindication to surgery as an initial management, regardless of the extent.10This report highlights the importance of using the complete clinicopathologic features, including tumor morphologic characteristics, immunohistochemical staining, and molecular profiling, to arrive at the correct diagnosis.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

case_info.explanation: The histopathological findings of the lymph node biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma with micropapillary features. The immunohistochemical staining was positive for GATA-3 and CK-7, along with 40% ER expression. Next-generation sequencing showed a microsatellite stable status and variations in theCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CAgenes. Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) with invasive ductal carcinoma and treated with systemic chemotherapy. It is important to note that the history of receiving the COVID-19 mRNA vaccine is a red herring in this case. It is challenging to differentiate between adnexal tumors and breast cancer when the patient presents with a cutaneous lesion of the breast. The current patient presented with a widespread rash, retracted nipple, and a peau d’orange appearance of the skin commonly seen in patients with IBC.1However, peau d’orange skin can also be seen in patients with cellulitis and radiation-induced lymphatic blockage.2The atypical cells obtained from a skin punch biopsy stained positive for GATA-3 and CK-7. GATA-3 belongs to the GATA family of zinc-finger transcription and is involved in the development and morphogenesis of breast tissue.3It is commonly expressed in ER-positive breast cancers. However, the expression of GATA-3 is not exclusive to breast cancer and has been reported in tumors of the salivary gland, urothelial system, skin and adnexa, mesothelioma, and pancreas.4Breast glands are considered to be modified and highly specialized apocrine glands. Hence, they share structural and functional homology with sweat glands.5 In addition to staining positive for GATA-3, adnexal tumors stain positive for P63, CK5/6, and CK-7. The clinical picture of the current patient was challenging due to the lack of a discrete breast mass and a positron emission tomography scan demonstrating an FDG-avid infiltrating mass in the chest wall and several lymph nodes in the axillary and internal mammary chain. A core-needle biopsy of the chest wall mass showed a similar staining pattern but stained positive for ER, unlike the punch biopsy of the skin, which was negative for both ER and progesterone receptor. However, a positive ER status alone is not sufficient to differentiate between an adnexal gland tumor and breast cancer.6The diagnosis was finally established with the results of the positive molecular testing forCDKN2,ERBB2, andPIK3CA. The phosphatidylinositol-3-kinases-CA (PIK3CA) variation is highly associated with ER-positive/ERBB2-negative breast cancer.7Likewise, ERBB2 (also known as HER2 or neu) is expressed in 30% of breast cancers.8Limited studies in patients with adnexal gland tumors reported no expression ofPIK3CAorERBB2in such patients.9Hence, the current patient’s pattern of the molecular profile of tumor tissue was most consistent with carcinoma of breast origin. Breast cancer in men accounts for 1% of all breast cancers.10Inflammatory breast cancer is an aggressive form of breast cancer that accounts for 2% to 4% of all breast cancers and 7% to 10% of breast cancer mortality in the US. The majority of men with breast cancer present with retroareolar mass. The usual presenting features are skin ulceration, retraction, bleeding from the nipple, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Inflammatory breast cancer in men is extremely rare, and the diagnosis is often made at an advanced stage due to lack of screening guidelines and confusion with gynecomastia (common in obese men).
